cls.function: Statement of opinion by the House
cls.banner: The Green New Deal resolution states an opinion of the House of Representatives. It is not a law. Even if the House approved it, no law would change. It would not order any agency to act or spend any money. It would also not go to the Senate or the President.
cls.checks: This analysis does not check the Green New Deal resolution for loopholes, enforcement or funding. The reason is that the resolution does not make anyone do anything. Instead, the analysis compares the resolution's goals with what it would really do. It also shows what a version with the force of law would need.
purpose.ladder.mechanism: The Green New Deal resolution would put the House on record. The House would be saying that the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal.
purpose.ladder.outcome: The Green New Deal resolution would give later bills a shared set of climate and economic goals. Those bills could then be measured against the goals.
purpose.ladder.aim: The Green New Deal resolution aims for net-zero greenhouse gas emissions. It also aims for millions of jobs and more economic security. It would reach these goals through a ten-year national effort.
promises.0.p: The title of the Green New Deal resolution says the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal.
promises.0.why: If the House approved the Green New Deal resolution, it would record the House's opinion that this duty exists. But a statement of opinion by the House has no power to create a legal duty.
promises.1.p: The first goal of the Green New Deal resolution is net-zero greenhouse gas emissions.
promises.1.why: In the Green New Deal resolution, net-zero emissions is only a goal. Nothing in the resolution limits, prices or controls emissions. The part that says what the House resolves gives no date for net-zero.
promises.2.p: News reports said the Green New Deal resolution was meant to end the country's greenhouse gas emissions in ten years.
promises.2.why: The Green New Deal resolution says its goals "should be accomplished through a 10-year national mobilization". That means a ten-year effort across the country. But the resolution does not say when the ten years start. It also does not say net-zero must be reached by the end of them.
promises.3.p: A 2023 Senate press release said the Green New Deal resolution would direct Congress to act.
promises.3.why: The Green New Deal resolution is an opinion of one chamber of Congress, the House. A statement like that cannot order Congress, a committee or a government agency to do anything.
promises.4.p: The Green New Deal resolution calls for millions of good jobs with high wages. It also calls for guaranteeing a job to everyone in the United States.
promises.4.why: The Green New Deal resolution sets up no program or agency for these jobs. It has no rules for who qualifies. It sets aside no money for the jobs or for the job guarantee.
promises.5.p: The Green New Deal resolution calls for meeting 100 percent of the country's power needs. That power would come from clean, renewable and zero-emission energy sources.
promises.5.why: The Green New Deal goal of 100 percent clean power has no standard and no deadline. The resolution also does not list which power sources count.
questions.0.q: What would legally change the day after the House approved the Green New Deal resolution?
questions.0.a: Nothing would legally change. The Green New Deal resolution speaks only for the House. It is not sent to the Senate or the President, and it is not a law. The Congressional Research Service is a research office that works for Congress. It notes that agencies may still watch such statements as a hint of what Congress might do later.
questions.1.q: Which words in the Green New Deal resolution would actually make each of its goals happen?
questions.1.a: None of the Green New Deal resolution's goals comes with words that would make it happen. The resolution uses the phrases "it is the duty", "should be accomplished" and "will require". These words state hopes, not orders. The resolution names no agency, sets aside no money and changes no existing law.
questions.2.q: Where does the wording of the Green New Deal resolution leave room for different readings of its goals?
questions.2.a: Four of the Green New Deal resolution's emissions goals apply only as far as is "technologically feasible". That means as far as technology makes possible. The net-zero goal has no date in the part that says what the House resolves. The resolution does not define "clean, renewable, and zero-emission" energy. So it does not settle whether nuclear power counts. It also does not settle whether fossil fuel power plants that capture their carbon count.
questions.3.q: Who does the Green New Deal resolution put in charge of reaching its goals?
questions.3.a: The Green New Deal resolution gives its duty only to "the Federal Government" as a whole. It does not name a department, an agency, an official or a committee to do the work.
questions.4.q: What would the Green New Deal resolution cost, and where would the money come from?
questions.4.a: The Green New Deal resolution gives no cost figure and provides no money. It would not spend anything. So no official cost estimate would be made for it.
questions.5.q: Has the text of the Green New Deal resolution ever been voted on in Congress?
questions.5.a: The House never voted on the Green New Deal resolution. The Senate majority leader, who leads the larger party in the Senate, brought the same text there. On March 26, 2019, a vote to take it up failed. The count was 0 in favor and 57 against, and 43 senators voted present.
questions.6.q: Have bills been introduced that would turn parts of the Green New Deal into law if they passed?
questions.6.a: Yes, separate bills like that have been introduced under the Green New Deal name. They include a Green New Deal for Public Housing Act and bills for a Civilian Climate Corps. A bill for a Green New Deal for public schools was introduced in July 2026. A search for loopholes applies to those bills, not to the resolution.
questions.7.q: What would a law need to actually reach the Green New Deal resolution's first goal of net-zero emissions?
questions.7.a: A law to reach the Green New Deal goal of net-zero emissions would need several things. It would need an emissions target with dates, written into law. It would need a named agency with power to set and enforce limits. It would need a source of money. It would also need a way to hold the government itself to the target. A table in the bigger picture panel lists these needs for each goal.
findings.G1.title: The Green New Deal resolution is a statement of opinion. It would not change any law.
findings.G1.plain: The Green New Deal resolution says "it is the sense of the House of Representatives". Those words mean the House is giving its opinion. Nothing that comes after them can make anyone do anything. That is true no matter what the rest of the wording says.
findings.G1.tech: The Green New Deal resolution is a type of measure that only the House votes on. It never goes to the President. The Congressional Research Service, a research office of Congress, says opinion statements like this are not legally binding. That means no one has to follow them. Every goal in the resolution falls under its opening words, which state the House's opinion.
findings.G1.use: A member of Congress can say that voting for or cosponsoring the Green New Deal resolution is action on climate. Yet no law has changed.
findings.G1.inq.q: What does the history of the Green New Deal resolution in Congress show about what kind of measure it is?
findings.G1.inq.items.0.h: The Green New Deal resolution was introduced in the House three times and never got a House vote.
findings.G1.inq.items.0.d: The Green New Deal resolution was first introduced as House Resolution 109 in 2019, with 101 cosponsors. It came back as House Resolution 332 in 2021 with 104. Then it came back as House Resolution 319 in 2023 with 96. Each time it was sent to a committee and went no further.
findings.G1.inq.items.1.h: The only vote on the Green New Deal text was set up by its opponents in the Senate.
findings.G1.inq.items.1.d: The Senate majority leader is the head of the larger party in the Senate. That leader introduced the same Green New Deal text there. A vote to take up the text failed 0 to 57, and 43 senators voted present.
findings.G1.inq.items.2.h: The Congressional Research Service is a research office for Congress. It says opinion statements like the Green New Deal resolution do not bind anyone by law.
findings.G1.inq.items.2.d: The Congressional Research Service does research for Congress. It says statements of opinion like the Green New Deal resolution are not legally binding. The reason is that they never go to the President. It also notes that agencies may watch them as a hint of what Congress might do.
findings.G1.inq.open: The cosponsor counts for the three versions of the Green New Deal resolution come from a secondhand table. They should be checked against the official records on Congress.gov.
findings.G1.two.dec: Will members of Congress write bills that put the Green New Deal resolution's climate and jobs goals into law?
findings.G1.two.views.0.why: Climate movement groups treat the Green New Deal resolution as a shared plan to organize around. They also see it as a promise to come back to.
findings.G1.two.views.1.why: The sponsors of the Green New Deal resolution can use it to gather cosponsors. They can do this without a cost estimate. They also do not have to face a filibuster, which is a long Senate speech used to block a vote.
findings.G1.two.views.2.why: Opponents in Congress can call a vote on a measure that binds no one, like the Green New Deal resolution. The vote puts members on record.
findings.G3.title: The Green New Deal resolution says the federal government has a duty to act. It puts no one in charge.
findings.G3.plain: The Green New Deal resolution says the federal government has a duty to create a Green New Deal. It does not name a department, an official or a deadline. So no one in particular would be in charge of that duty.
findings.G3.tech: Laws that require action always name a specific official. For example, a law may say "the Administrator shall" act, which means that official must act. The Green New Deal resolution names only "the Federal Government" as a whole. The whole government cannot be ordered, sued or given money as one body.
findings.G4.title: The Green New Deal resolution only says its goals "should" be met in ten years. It sets no start date.
findings.G4.plain: The Green New Deal resolution says its goals "should be accomplished" through a ten-year national effort. "Should" is a suggestion, not an order. The resolution also does not say when the ten years begin.
findings.G4.tech: When laws are written, "should" suggests an action but does not require it. The phrase "10-year national mobilization" in the Green New Deal resolution has no start date. A mobilization is a large effort across the country. The 2021 and 2023 versions of the resolution used the same ten-year wording.
findings.G4.use: The Green New Deal resolution sets no start date for its ten years. So anyone talking about it can say the ten years begin whenever they like.
findings.G5.title: The Green New Deal resolution limits four emissions goals to what technology makes possible. No one is named to decide.
findings.G5.plain: The Green New Deal resolution has goals for infrastructure, factories, farming and transportation. For each one, the goal is to remove emissions "as much as technologically feasible". That means as much as technology makes possible. The resolution does not say who gets to decide what is possible.
findings.G5.tech: In a real law, a limit like "technologically feasible" gives power to whoever judges what is possible. That person decides how much must be done. The choice is usually based on facts from the industry that is being regulated. In the Green New Deal resolution, the phrase appears four times. It covers infrastructure, manufacturing, farming and transportation.
findings.G5.use: Suppose a later law copied the Green New Deal phrase "technologically feasible". Then each industry's emissions goal would be only as strong as the choice about what is possible.
findings.G6.title: The Green New Deal resolution calls for net-zero emissions with no deadline, starting point or way to count them.
findings.G6.plain: The first goal of the Green New Deal resolution is net-zero greenhouse gas emissions. The resolution does not say by when. It does not say how emissions would be measured. It also does not say what counts as an offset, which is a step that makes up for emissions.
findings.G6.tech: The Green New Deal resolution opens with "Whereas" paragraphs that give its reasons. They mention a need for net-zero emissions worldwide by 2050. The part that says what the House resolves ties the goals to a ten-year effort. But it sets no date for net-zero. The word "net" suggests that some emissions can be removed or made up for. The resolution does not say what counts.
findings.G6.use: Supporters and critics can each describe the Green New Deal net-zero goal in their own way. Both can point to the resolution's words.
findings.G6.two.dec: Would a later law based on the Green New Deal resolution set a date to reach net-zero emissions?
findings.G6.two.views.0.why: Climate movement groups would want a deadline for the Green New Deal goal of net-zero emissions.
findings.G7.title: The Green New Deal resolution does not say which energy counts as clean, or if nuclear power does.
findings.G7.plain: The Green New Deal resolution calls for all of the country's power to come from "clean, renewable, and zero-emission" sources. It does not say if a source must be all three or just one. That choice decides whether nuclear power counts.
findings.G7.tech: Nuclear power plants give off no emissions, but they are not renewable. Renewable means the source does not run out. Fossil fuel plants that capture their carbon may be neither. Leaving the list open in the Green New Deal resolution may keep supporters with different views together. That is why this finding is treated as a trade-off.
findings.G7.use: The Green New Deal resolution leaves the list of clean energy sources open. So a later bill that would actually become law would have to decide which sources count.
findings.G8.title: The Green New Deal resolution talks about guaranteeing everyone a job. It creates no program, rules or money for it.
findings.G8.plain: The Green New Deal resolution speaks of "guaranteeing a job" to all people in the United States. A real job guarantee needs a program, rules and money. It also needs an employer of last resort. That means an employer that hires people who cannot find other work. The resolution has none of these.
findings.G8.tech: The same is true of other goals in the Green New Deal resolution. It calls for "guaranteeing universal access to clean water", which means clean water for all. It also calls for giving everyone "high-quality health care". In a measure that binds no one, these phrases only state goals.
findings.G8.use: Someone can quote the word "guaranteeing" from the Green New Deal resolution. They can make it sound as if a job guarantee were already law.
findings.G10.title: The Green New Deal resolution says future infrastructure bills should deal with climate change. Its opinion does not bind them.
findings.G10.plain: The Green New Deal resolution calls for any infrastructure bill in Congress to deal with climate change. Infrastructure means things like roads and bridges. But a statement of opinion by one chamber of Congress cannot control what later bills say.
findings.G10.tech: The House and the Senate can each set official rules for their own work, and those rules do bind them. For example, a rule can let a member object to a bill that breaks it. A statement of opinion like the Green New Deal resolution is not one of those rules.
findings.G12.title: The Green New Deal resolution puts its 1.5 degree warming limit and 2050 date only in its opening reasons.
findings.G12.plain: The Green New Deal resolution opens with paragraphs that start with "Whereas". Those paragraphs give the House's reasons. Specific numbers, such as the 1.5 degree limit and the 2050 date, appear only there. They are not part of what the House actually resolves.
findings.G12.tech: Opening statements of reasons can help explain a measure. But they do not create any rights or duties. In the Green New Deal resolution, the most specific targets are outside the part that says what the House resolves.
findings.G12.use: People often quote numbers from the opening paragraphs of the Green New Deal resolution. They quote them as if they were promises.
findings.G9.title: The Green New Deal resolution gives no cost estimate. It provides no money for any of its goals.
findings.G9.plain: The Green New Deal resolution sets goals that would take very large public spending. It gives no cost figure and sets aside no money. A statement of opinion could not set aside money anyway.
findings.G9.tech: Only a bill or other measure that becomes law can approve or set aside federal money. The Green New Deal resolution mentions "adequate capital", meaning enough money. It says this could come through community grants, public banks and other public funding. But it gives no amounts.
findings.G9.use: Supporters and opponents make claims about what the Green New Deal would cost. No one can check those claims against the resolution. It has no cost figures.
findings.G14.title: The House never voted on the Green New Deal resolution. A Senate vote on its text failed 0 to 57.
findings.G14.plain: The House never voted on the Green New Deal resolution. The Senate majority leader, who leads the larger party there, brought the same text to the Senate. The Senate then voted on whether to take it up. That vote failed 0 to 57, and 43 senators voted present.
findings.G14.tech: In the Senate, the same Green New Deal text was a joint resolution. That is a type of measure that can become law. Supporters of the House resolution called the vote a tactic and voted present. This shows how a measure that binds no one can be used to put members on record.
findings.G14.use: Either side can use the Senate vote on the Green New Deal text. One side can call it proof of no support. The other side can call it proof of a sham process.
findings.G13.title: Separate bills using the Green New Deal name would change the law if passed. The resolution itself would not.
findings.G13.plain: Some people look for measures that would actually change the law. They should look at separate bills that use the Green New Deal name. Examples include bills on public housing and a Civilian Climate Corps.
findings.G13.tech: Those Green New Deal bills are regular bills in the House and Senate. People would have to follow them if they became law. They can be checked for loopholes in the usual way.
bigger.lead: The Green New Deal resolution names almost every part of the federal climate and economic agenda. But it is only a statement of opinion, so it changes none of them. The first table shows what the resolution names. The second table shows what a measure with the force of law would need for each goal.
bigger.map.0.note: The Green New Deal resolution makes net-zero emissions a goal. But it sets no limit, price or standard for emissions.
bigger.map.1.note: The Green New Deal resolution calls for power that is 100 percent clean, renewable and zero-emission. It does not say which sources count.
bigger.map.2.note: In each of these areas, the Green New Deal resolution limits its emissions goal. It asks only for what technology makes possible.
bigger.map.3.note: The Green New Deal resolution does not say how much public money it would take or where that money would come from.
bigger.map.4.note: The Green New Deal resolution speaks of guarantees for jobs, wages and workers' rights. But it sets up no programs to deliver them.
bigger.map.5.part: Health care, housing and economic security
bigger.map.5.note: The Green New Deal resolution lists health care, housing and economic security. It says a Green New Deal will require them.
bigger.map.6.note: Later laws on clean energy spending and taxes were passed as separate bills. Sponsors of the 2023 version of the Green New Deal resolution pointed to those laws.
stake.clim.want: Climate movement groups want a shared plan and a public promise to build on. Movement groups backed the Green New Deal resolution.
stake.labor.want: Labor unions want guaranteed jobs and wages. They also want protection for workers in industries that would shrink. Some unions backed the Green New Deal resolution.
stake.foss.role: Fossil fuel companies and their workers
stake.foss.want: Fossil fuel companies and their workers do not want a required end to fossil fuels. If one comes, they want it to take as long as possible.
stake.util.want: Electric utilities want clear rules on which power sources will count, and time to build.
stake.nuc.want: Supporters of nuclear energy want it to be clear that nuclear power counts as clean.
stake.fisc.role: Members of Congress focused on spending
stake.fisc.want: Members of Congress focused on spending want a cost figure first. They also want a source of money before any promise is made.
stake.front.role: Communities the resolution calls frontline and vulnerable
stake.front.want: Communities the Green New Deal resolution calls frontline and vulnerable want to come first when money is spent. They want a rule that can be enforced, not only a mention.
stake.spon.want: The sponsors of the Green New Deal resolution want it to set a direction. They want later bills to carry it out.
stake.opp.want: Opponents in Congress want a recorded vote that puts supporters on record. Opponents were the ones who set up the Senate vote on the Green New Deal text.
stake.crs.role: Nonpartisan analysts who work for Congress
stake.crs.want: Nonpartisan analysts who work for Congress take no side. They say opinion statements like the Green New Deal resolution have no force of law.
stake.tex.role: A judge who reads laws by their exact words
stake.tex.want: A judge who reads laws by their exact words applies those words as written. That judge will not fill in what Congress left out.
stake.pur.role: A judge who reads laws by their purpose
stake.pur.want: A judge who reads laws by their purpose settles doubts in favor of what the law was trying to do.
stake.olc.want: A person who drafts laws wants every key term defined. They want every reference checked. They also want every link to existing law clearly stated.
conf_note: The Green New Deal resolution gives no job to any agency or official. So no one is in charge whose independence could be checked. A later law that carried out its goals would need this check.
